group.name: Far-Future Space Opera
group.tagline: Humanity survives the next ten thousand years and spreads across the galaxy.
group.question: What does a galactic civilisation thousands of years downstream of us look like?
group.divergenceMechanism: A founding rupture — often no longer remembered — after which humanity's future runs millennia beyond our own.

lineages.title: Star Trek
lineages.creator: Gene Roddenberry

divergence.label: First Contact, 5 April 2063
divergence.delta: Real: nobody has flown faster than light and no alien ship has ever answered a signal from Earth. Fiction: Zefram Cochrane's warp flight from a converted missile silo in Montana is picked up by a passing Vulcan survey ship, and Earth's isolation ends inside one lifetime — the branch runs on to a United Federation of Planets, a five-year mission, and a Federation still rebuilding in the 32nd century.
divergence.inUniverse: 2063 (Star Trek dates itself in real-world years; stardates are a separate in-story convention)
divergence.note: The one branch in this group that needs no conversion: it is dated in our own calendar, and 5 April 2063 at Bozeman, Montana is stated on screen in Star Trek: First Contact and celebrated in-universe as First Contact Day. Strictly, the fiction's Earth already differs from ours earlier — the Eugenics Wars of the 1990s, the Bell Riots of 2024 and World War III of 2026–2053 all sit in the prehistory window below — but 2063 is the franchise's own threshold, the moment the human story stops being a lonely one. The 2009 reboot is a separate in-universe branch, not this one: Nero and Spock fall back from 2387 to 2233, and Nero's attack on the USS Kelvin forks the 'Kelvin timeline' off the prime timeline; its fork point is 2233 and its inciting event is the 2387 Hobus supernova.

ending.why: Across a thousand years the Federation falls apart and is rebuilt; the arc bends toward a plural, curious, post-scarcity civilisation.

events.title: The Eugenics Wars
events.description: Genetically engineered 'Augments' led by Khan Noonien Singh seize power over a quarter of Earth and are overthrown after four years of war, after which the survivors flee the solar system in the sleeper ship Botany Bay.
events.note: Genuinely contested across canon levels. TOS 'Space Seed' (1967) dates the Eugenics Wars to the 1990s, which real history has now falsified; DS9 'Doctor Bashir, I Presume?' moves them to the 22nd century, and Star Trek: Strange New Worlds (2022) places a young Khan in the 2020s. The 1990s date is the original and best-known reading, and it is the earliest point at which the fiction's Earth stops matching ours.
events.binWhy: Augmented humans seize a quarter of the Earth before being overthrown.

facets.change: nations → a quarter of Earth under augmented rulers, then overthrown

events.title: The Bell Riots
events.description: In a bankrupt San Francisco, the forced encampment of the unemployed in 'sanctuary districts' erupts into a riot whose suppression breaks the political will behind the camps — the fiction's hinge on the road back to a unified Earth.
events.note: DS9 'Past Tense' (1995) named 2024 as the year; the date has since passed in real history without the events depicted, which makes it a clean marker of how far the branch has already drifted.
events.binWhy: The ruled revolt against those who hold power over them.

facets.change: internment tolerated → internment ended

events.title: World War III and the post-atomic horror
events.description: A third world war fought with nuclear, biological and genetic weapons kills some 600 million people and ends with Earth's major cities in ruins; the decades of 'post-atomic horror' that follow are the world Zefram Cochrane grows up in, and the world the Vulcans initially decline to rescue.
events.note: Dated by ENT 'In a Mirror, Darkly' and Star Trek: First Contact, which place the war in the 2026–2053 window; TOS had earlier put it in the 1990s.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: tension → nuclear, biological and genetic war

events.title: Cochrane's warp flight and first contact
events.description: Zefram Cochrane's converted missile Phoenix makes humanity's first faster-than-light flight; the warp signature is detected by a Vulcan survey ship, which lands at Bozeman, Montana, and greets humanity — the branch point of the whole archetype.
events.note: Star Trek: First Contact (1996). The date is April 5, fixed on screen and by the in-universe holiday First Contact Day.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: alone → first faster-than-light flight, met on landing

events.title: Terra Nova, Earth's first extrasolar colony
events.description: Six years after first contact, the colony ship SS Conestoga is launched to Terra Nova — the first human settlement outside the solar system, and the template for the wave of colonisation that follows.
events.note: ENT 'Terra Nova' (2001).
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: one system → first settlement outside it

events.title: Enterprise NX-01 launches
events.description: Earth's first deep-range warp-5 starship leaves spacedock under Jonathan Archer, carrying the first human crew into the wider galaxy and into the diplomacy that makes a federation thinkable.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: home system → first deep-range ship leaves

events.title: The Earth–Romulan War
events.description: Earth and its allies fight the Romulan Star Empire to a standstill with primitive nuclear-tipped weapons and no visual contact; the war ends at the Battle of Cheron and produces the Romulan Neutral Zone.
events.note: The four-year span is established by the Okuda chronology and referenced on screen; the war itself has never been dramatised in full, so its internal events are largely unchronicled.
events.binWhy: A war fought blind to a standstill.

facets.change: frontier tension → war fought blind to a standstill

events.title: The United Federation of Planets is founded
events.description: Earth, Vulcan, Andoria and Tellar sign a charter at San Francisco, creating a multi-species federation with a single Starfleet — the archetype's model answer to what a galactic civilisation should be.
events.binWhy: Independent powers become one polity.

facets.change: allies → one charter, one fleet

events.title: Nero's arrival forks the Kelvin timeline
events.description: The Romulan mining ship Narada and the ambassador Spock fall through a red-matter black hole from 2387 into 2233; Nero's attack on the USS Kelvin kills George Kirk and creates the 'Kelvin timeline', the separate branch in which the 2009–2016 films take place and in which James T. Kirk is born in a shuttlecraft.
events.note: A distinct in-universe branch, not the lineage's divergence: its cause is the 2387 Hobus event listed below, which lies later in the prime timeline's own order. Star Trek (2009).
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: one history → a ship from the future forks it

events.title: The five-year mission
events.description: The Constitution-class USS Enterprise under James T. Kirk is sent out on a five-year mission of exploration; its encounters — with the Organians, the Romulans, the Guardian of Forever — make the Federation a galactic power rather than a regional club.
events.note: TOS itself gave only stardates; the 2265–2270 span is the standard Okuda chronology, now effectively canon.
events.binWhy: The ship is sent out to explore and makes the Federation a power.

facets.change: known space → sent out to explore

events.title: The Khitomer Accords
events.description: After the Klingon moon Praxis explodes and bankrupts the Empire, the Federation and the Klingons sign an alliance at Khitomer, ending seventy years of cold war and setting up the long peace of the 24th century.
events.note: Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country (1991).
events.binWhy: Enemies sign a treaty, truce or alliance.

facets.change: seventy years of cold war → alliance after the enemy's disaster

events.title: The Federation at its height
events.description: A century after Khitomer the Federation has hundreds of member worlds, a lasting peace with the Klingons and a new Enterprise — and meets both Q and the Borg, the two forces that will define the next decade.
events.binWhy: Hundreds of member worlds and a lasting peace, just before the Borg.

facets.change: peace → the federation at its height

events.title: The Dominion War
events.description: The Federation Alliance fights the Dominion and its Cardassian allies across the Alpha Quadrant in the largest war the branch has yet shown, ending with the fall of Cardassia and the Founders' surrender.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: rivalry → the largest war, ending in the enemy's surrender

events.title: The Hobus supernova destroys Romulus
events.description: A supernova destroys the Romulan homeworld and its empire's heartland; the failed evacuation, and the red-matter attempt to stop the blast, are the inciting event of the Kelvin branch and the reason the Romulan state is a ruin by the 25th century.
events.note: Star Trek (2009) opens here; Star Trek: Picard shows the political aftermath.
events.binWhy: A homeworld and its heartland are destroyed.

facets.change: an empire's heartland → destroyed by its star

events.title: The Burn
events.description: A resonance catastrophe destroys most of the galaxy's dilithium in an instant, ending warp travel and with it the United Federation of Planets, which fragments into isolated worlds for a century.
events.note: Star Trek: Discovery season 3 (2020); the cause is revealed as a Kelpien's grief-driven psychic shock.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: faster-than-light civilisation → its fuel destroyed in an instant

events.title: The Federation rebuilds in the 32nd century
events.description: A thousand years after Kirk, the USS Discovery arrives in a galaxy of scattered worlds where the Federation is a rump of a few dozen members, and becomes the instrument of its reconnection.
events.note: Star Trek: Discovery seasons 3–5 (2020–2024).
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: scattered worlds → the federation reconnects

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's cleanest and most load-bearing case: a founding rupture in our own measurable future, after which the fiction's history is simply our history continued — no new calendar, no conversion, just the real years 2063, 2161, 2265, 2293 and onward. It is the group's optimistic pole: the far future here is a federation of species rather than an empire, and it is the one branch whose deep time (the 32nd century) is still recognisably descended from our own institutions. Tier coverage is lopsided by construction rather than by omission: the lineage has no T4 events at all, because before 1900 its history is literally our history — the fiction adds nothing to the record until the Eugenics Wars of the 1990s. Its mass sits in T2 (2000–2300), which is exactly where a 1960s television future put its first contact, its Romulan War and its Federation, and it reaches T1 only with the 24th century and beyond.

lineages.title: Star Wars
lineages.creator: George Lucas

divergence.label: The founding of the Galactic Republic
divergence.delta: Real: 23,023 BCE is the Upper Palaeolithic - no cities, no writing, no metals, no wheels. Fiction: in that same era a Galactic Republic is founded that will last 25,000 years, hold a galaxy together through a Jedi Order, fall to an Empire, and be succeeded by a First Order. The fork is not a change to our history; it is an entire galactic civilisation inserted into our Stone Age.
divergence.inUniverse: 25,000 BBY (BBY/ABY = years before/after the Battle of Yavin)
divergence.note: Conversion, stated explicitly: the Battle of Yavin (year 0 of the BBY/ABY system) is mapped to 1977, the release year and story present of the original film, so real = 1977 - BBY before Yavin and 1977 + ABY after it. The founding figure is the one printed and current-canon sources give: The Star Wars Book and Star Wars: Timelines place the Old Republic's founding at c. 25,000 BBY, as did the Legends reference books (The Essential Guide to Warfare, The New Essential Chronology, The Essential Atlas). The frequently quoted 25,053 BBY is web-only Legends material traced to a Star Wars: The Old Republic HoloNet entry and could not be found in any printed reference book - the live and archived HoloNet pages say only 'more than twenty thousand years' - and it would move this date 53 years earlier, to 23,076 BCE. Note the direction, which is the opposite of what an early draft of the brief assumed: 25,000 BBY is 23,023 years BEFORE the 1977 anchor, so the whole branch lies in our deep past, which is exactly what 'a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away' asserts. Nothing in Star Wars canon ties the BBY/ABY calendar to Earth - canon has no Earth and no Milky Way - so this is a placement convention, not a continuity claim.

ending.why: Empire, Republic, First Order: the galaxy keeps relapsing into tyranny and keeps throwing it off; the saga as told ends with the tyrant's second fall.

events.title: The Galactic Republic is founded
events.description: A Republic of member worlds is founded and its capital eventually settles on Coruscant; over the next 25,000 years it grows into a galaxy-spanning state guarded by a Jedi Order, and its origins fade into legend.
events.note: No film dates this. Printed reference books and the current canon chronology both give c. 25,000 BBY; a web-only Legends figure of 25,053 BBY is noted in the divergence note.
events.binWhy: Independent powers become one polity.

facets.change: member worlds → one republic

events.title: The Ruusan Reformations and the fall of the Sith
events.description: The last Jedi-Sith war ends with the Sith destroyed at Ruusan, the Republic disarmed and its Supreme Chancellor's powers cut back, and the Sith survivor Darth Bane taking the order underground under the Rule of Two - the rearrangement the prequel-era Republic inherits a thousand years later.
events.note: Contested across canon levels. Canon dates the end of the Jedi-Sith War and the restoration of the modern Republic to 1,032 BBY (Star Wars: Timelines; The Star Wars Book) but gives the Ruusan Reformations no date at all; Legends reference books date the Reformations to 1,000 BBY, where the Republic Measures and Standards Bureau reset the calendar's year zero to the battle. I use the canon 1,032 BBY, which converts to 945 CE; the Legends date would be 977 CE.
events.binWhy: The Republic is disarmed by law and the Sith are driven underground.

facets.change: militarised republic → disarmed by law; the enemy goes underground

events.title: The High Republic at its height
events.description: The Republic and the Jedi Order stand at their zenith and expand into the Outer Rim from the Starlight Beacon; within a few years the Nihil marauders and a run of catastrophes bring the era down.
events.note: Date from the Star Wars: The High Republic publishing initiative (2021 onwards), which is canon but set two centuries before the films; nothing in the nine-film saga references it.
events.binWhy: The Republic and the Jedi at their zenith, just before the fall.

facets.change: expansion → the republic and its order at their zenith

events.title: The Invasion of Naboo
events.description: The Trade Federation blockades and invades Naboo; the crisis exposes the Republic's paralysis, forces a vote of no confidence in the Chancellor and lifts Senator Palpatine to power - the first move in the Sith plan to take the galaxy.
events.binWhy: A manufactured crisis lifts Palpatine to power.

facets.change: a trade dispute → blockade, invasion, and a new chancellor

events.title: The Clone Wars begin
events.description: The Separatist crisis becomes open war at Geonosis; the Republic fields a clone army and the Jedi become generals in a conflict engineered on both sides by Darth Sidious.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: separatist crisis → open civil war

events.title: Order 66 and the fall of the Republic
events.description: The clone army turns on the Jedi and the Republic is reconstituted as the first Galactic Empire under Emperor Palpatine in the Proclamation of the New Order; the survivors of the Order go into hiding for two decades.
events.note: Order 66, the Great Jedi Purge and the Proclamation of the New Order are all dated 19 BBY by Star Wars: Timelines and Star Wars: Galactic Atlas.
events.binWhy: The Republic is reconstituted as an Empire in one proclamation.

facets.change: republic → empire in one proclamation

events.title: The Rebel Alliance is declared
events.description: Delegates from scattered rebel cells sign the Corellian Treaty and declare the Alliance to Restore the Republic - the political birth of the Rebellion that will fight the Empire openly.
events.note: Star Wars Rebels, 'Secret Cargo' (2017), dates the declaration to 2 BBY.
events.binWhy: The ruled revolt against those who hold power over them.

facets.change: scattered cells → an alliance declared

events.title: Alderaan is destroyed
events.description: The Empire obliterates Alderaan as a demonstration of the Death Star's power, killing its entire population and driving Princess Leia into the Rebel Alliance's arms.
events.note: One of the few genuinely odd places in Star Wars dating. Star Wars: Galactic Atlas: Updated Edition (2025) and Timelines (2023) put Alderaan's destruction in 1 BBY and the Battle of Yavin in year 0, even though in the story the two are days apart; the 2016 Galactic Atlas and the Legends continuity put both in 0 BBY. I follow the current canon numbering and keep them as separate years, which is why they are two events here rather than one.
events.binWhy: A planet's population is killed as a demonstration.

facets.change: a world → destroyed as a demonstration

events.title: The Battle of Yavin
events.description: The Rebellion destroys the first Death Star at Yavin, the battle that becomes the zero point of the galaxy's calendar and the story present of the 1977 film - and, in this dataset, the anchor for the whole conversion.
events.inUniverse: year 0 (0 BBY; Lucasfilm now prints simply '0')
events.note: The zero point of the ABY-BBY system is high confidence; the notation is not, since Lucasfilm staff have said 'there is no 0 BBY' while '0 BBY' remains in print.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: the weapon → destroyed by the rebellion

events.title: The Battle of Hoth
events.description: The Empire finds the Rebel base on Hoth and routs it; the Alliance scatters across the galaxy, and Luke Skywalker goes to seek the last Jedi Master.
events.binWhy: The rebellion is routed and scattered.

facets.change: rebel base → routed and scattered

events.title: The Battle of Endor and the death of the Emperor
events.description: The Rebel fleet destroys the second Death Star over Endor while Darth Vader kills the Emperor and dies himself; within days the Empire fractures into competing warlords.
events.binWhy: The fleet destroys the weapon and the Emperor dies with it.

facets.change: empire → its ruler dies with the second weapon

events.title: The Battle of Jakku and the fall of the Empire
events.description: The last great Imperial fleet is destroyed over the desert world of Jakku and the remnant signs the Galactic Concordance, ending the civil war and binding the Empire to disarm and withdraw into the Unknown Regions.
events.note: Battle of Jakku and Galactic Concordance both dated 5 ABY (Star Wars: Galactic Atlas; Star Wars: Timelines); Lost Stars puts the Empire's final defeat one year and four days after Endor.
events.binWhy: The last Imperial fleet is destroyed and the remnant signs the Concordance.

facets.change: imperial remnant → destroyed; disarmed by treaty

events.title: The First Order declares itself
events.description: The Imperial remnant that withdrew into the Unknown Regions after Jakku - reorganised since 21 ABY as the First Order - goes public, and Centrist systems secede from the New Republic; the cold war that ends at Starkiller Base begins here.
events.note: Inferred: The Rise of Skywalker: The Visual Dictionary says the First Order was publicly formed five years before the Starkiller Incident, which Star Wars: Galactic Atlas dates to 34 ABY. Star Wars: Timelines dates the First Order's establishment to 21 ABY.
events.binWhy: The remnant goes public, systems secede and a cold war begins.

facets.change: hidden remnant → declares itself; systems secede

events.title: The First Order strikes
events.description: The First Order destroys the New Republic's capital system with Starkiller Base and is destroyed in turn within days; the galaxy is at war again, and the last Jedi goes into exile.
events.note: Hosnian Cataclysm and Battle of Starkiller Base both dated 34 ABY by Star Wars: Galactic Atlas.
events.binWhy: A capital system is destroyed and the galaxy is at war again.

facets.change: cold war → the capital system destroyed

lineages.groupingNote: The group's inverse case and its most popular one: everything the archetype asks for - a founding rupture no longer remembered, a 25,000-year-old Republic, a fall into empire, a dark age, a return - happens not downstream of us but upstream. Star Wars is 'a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away'; it never claims to be Earth's future, so it cannot be converted into our years by continuity, only by convention, and the convention used here (0 BBY = 1977, the original film's story present) places the entire saga in our past. That produces the one genuinely surprising shape in this group: the lineage has no T1 events at all, because even its furthest future converts to 2011 CE. Its deep history (the Republic's founding, the Ruusan Reformations, the High Republic) is T4; its film-era present is overwhelmingly T3 - eight events - because pinning each film's story present to the 1977 anchor drops them into the 20th century; and only the First Order's rise and war reach T2. Empty tiers are left empty rather than padded, and the fiction is silent about Earth entirely: there is no T4 material about our own history to record because Star Wars never touches it. phaseIsAuthored is set on this lineage because a single divergence year cannot classify a branch that runs 25,000 years: the fork is the Republic's founding, which on the real axis is also the Upper Palaeolithic, and every later beat is deep in the branch's own history even when it lands in our recorded 20th century; phases are assigned by that narrative judgement rather than derived.

lineages.title: Dune
lineages.creator: Frank Herbert

divergence.label: The Butlerian Jihad
divergence.delta: Real: the year 16,000 is empty - no human being has ever lived then and our record stops in the 21st century. Fiction: in the same era humanity turns on the thinking machines that had come to rule it, and the two-generation crusade that follows becomes the founding rupture of a galactic civilisation. Its commandment, 'Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind', still governs the Imperium ten thousand years later, and the Guild calendar that dates every event below is counted from the settlement that ended it.
divergence.inUniverse: 201 B.G. (Before Guild; the calendar's year zero is the Spacing Guild's monopoly)
divergence.note: A projection, and flagged as one. No Frank Herbert text, appendix or interview gives a real-world year for Dune: the novel's own glossary defines the epoch (B.G./A.G. = before/after the Spacing Guild's monopoly) and Appendix IV dates the story to 10,191 A.G., but nothing bridges that to Earth. The bridge used here is the non-canon Dune Encyclopedia, the only reference work with a Terran chronology: it dates the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588 CE) to 14,512 B.G. and the first use of atomics in war (1945 CE) to 14,255 B.G., which puts the calendar epoch at roughly 16,100-16,200 CE. I take A.G. 0 = 16,200 CE, so the Jihad begins at 15,999 (rounded to 16,000 here), the novel's 10,191 A.G. falls at 26,391 and Chapterhouse at 15,240 A.G. at 41,440. Uncertainty is about a century from the Encyclopedia's own disagreeing anchors alone, and much more if the non-canon material is rejected: the canon-only reading is that interstellar travel had been underway for 'one hundred and ten centuries' before the Jihad, which supports 'tens of thousands of years in the future' and fixes no date. Standard Years are also some twenty hours shorter than Terran years, worth centuries of drift across 10,191 of them. Herbert himself never said.

ending.why: Herbert died with Duncan and Sheeana fleeing into an unmapped universe while the Honored Matres and the Bene Gesserit merge; nothing is settled.

events.title: Terran atomics, dated from the far end
events.description: The Dune Encyclopedia's Terran chronology dates the first use of atomics in war to 14,255 B.G. - our own 1945 - and threads Alexander, the Armada and a Golden Age of Invention through the same B.G. sequence. It is the only place in Dune reference material where our history is given a date in the fiction's own calendar.
events.note: Non-canon and internally shaky: the Encyclopedia's Terran anchors imply a calendar epoch of 16,100 CE from the 1588 entry and 16,200 CE from the 1945 entry. Its inclusion here is deliberate - it is the single thread tying this branch back to our era - but no canon source dates Earth history at all.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: conventional war → atomics used

events.title: Dune is published
events.description: Frank Herbert's Dune appears, the real-world origin of the branch and the anchor without which none of these dates could be plotted at all.
events.note: A real-world publication event, not an in-universe one; it sits in the branch's prehistory because the fiction's history has not forked from ours in 1965.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Butlerian Jihad
events.description: Humanity turns on the thinking machines: the crusade against computers, thinking machines and conscious robots runs for two generations, ends with the injunction 'Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind', and becomes the founding rupture of all later human civilisation - the Orange Catholic Bible, the Great Convention and the Guild's monopoly all grow out of it.
events.note: The in-universe dates are canon (the novel's own glossary dates the Jihad 201-108 B.G.); the real-world year is the projection described in the divergence note.
events.binWhy: Humanity rises against the machines that governed it.

facets.change: machine rule → machines destroyed and forbidden

events.title: The Battle of Corrin
events.description: The space battle near Sigma Draconis settles the ascendancy of House Corrino over the last armies of the Jihad and the remnants of the machine empire; the Corrino Empire begins eighty-eight years before the Guild's calendar does.
events.note: 88 B.G. is canon (novel glossary). The real year follows the projection.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: post-jihad struggle → one house ascends

events.title: The Spacing Guild takes its monopoly
events.description: The Guild's monopoly on space travel, transport and interstellar banking begins and is taken as year zero of the Imperial calendar; CHOAM is chartered in the same settlement. No ship moves without the Guild's consent for the next ten thousand years, and every date in Dune is measured from here.
events.note: The epoch is canon by definition (novel glossary: 'The Guild monopoly ... is taken as the beginning point of the Imperial Calendar'). The Dune Encyclopedia adds that the Guild existed as an organisation from 78 B.G., so the monopoly and the founding are different events.
events.binWhy: One body takes a monopoly on all travel and banking.

facets.change: open travel → one body's monopoly on all movement and banking

events.title: House Atreides takes Arrakis
events.description: House Atreides is given Arrakis and destroyed within the year: Leto I dies, Paul and Jessica flee to the Fremen, and Alia is born. It is the opening of Dune and the hinge on which the Imperium's ten-thousand-year-old order turns.
events.note: 10,191 A.G. is canon: Appendix IV dates Leto I (10,140-10,191) and the novel's chapter epigraphs give the same year. The real year is projected.
events.binWhy: The Duke is killed within the year and his house destroyed; the heir flees.

facets.change: a great house → given a planet and destroyed within the year

events.title: Paul Muad'Dib becomes Emperor
events.description: Shaddam IV abdicates and Paul takes the throne; his Fremen legions carry a jihad across the Imperium that kills billions in his name and breaks the Corrino-Guild-CHOAM settlement that had held the peace for ten thousand years.
events.note: The A.G. year comes from the Dune Encyclopedia and wiki chronologies, not from the novel, which gives only the sequence; the real year inherits that plus the projection.
events.binWhy: The prophet takes the throne and his legions carry a jihad.

facets.change: emperor → a prophet takes the throne; his legions carry a jihad

events.title: Dune Messiah
events.description: Twelve years into Paul's reign a conspiracy of the Bene Gesserit, the Guild and the Tleilaxu breaks the prophet; Paul walks blind into the desert and the Imperial centre of gravity shifts to his sister and his twin children.
events.note: The twelve-year interval is stated in the novel; the A.G. years are reference-book reconstructions.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: prophet-emperor → broken by conspiracy, walks into the desert

events.title: Children of Dune: Leto II takes the throne
events.description: Leto II begins his metamorphosis into the sandworm and becomes Emperor; his reign will run for three and a half thousand years and will end the spice's dependence on a single planet.
events.note: Nine years after Dune Messiah per the novel; the A.G. year is a reference-book reconstruction.
events.binWhy: The heir takes the throne and begins his transformation.

facets.change: regency → the heir takes the throne and begins to change

events.title: The death of the God Emperor
events.description: Leto II dies after 3,500 years as the God Emperor; his death releases the Scattering, in which trillions of humans flee beyond the Imperium's reach, and no single power can ever again hold the species.
events.note: The 3,500-year reign is canon; the end year is not agreed - the Dune Encyclopedia has 13,724, wiki chronologies 13,727-13,728, and 10,219 plus 3,500 gives 13,719. Herbert's own books also contain a contradictory epigraph ('ten thousand years since Leto II began his metamorphosis') in Heretics.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: 3,500 years of one ruler → dies; humanity scatters

events.title: The Honored Matres return
events.description: The Honored Matres come back from the Scattering and burn Arrakis; fifteen hundred years after Leto II's death the Bene Gesserit face a force bred in the wilderness beyond the old Imperium.
events.note: The 1,500-year interval is stated in reference material; the A.G. year is wiki-derived.
events.binWhy: An enemy returns from beyond the frontier and burns the capital.

facets.change: scattered humanity → returns as an enemy and burns the capital

events.title: Chapterhouse: Dune
events.description: The Bene Gesserit, holding the last sandworms on Chapterhouse, fight the Honored Matres to a standstill and begin building a new sisterhood and a new Arrakis from scratch - the last point Frank Herbert's own chronology reaches.
events.note: Weakest date in the lineage: wiki-derived only.
events.binWhy: The sisterhood fights the invaders to a standstill.

facets.change: invasion → fought to a standstill; a new order begins

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's darkest case and its clearest remembered rupture: a galactic civilisation twenty-odd thousand years downstream of us whose founding event - the Butlerian Jihad against thinking machines - survives only as religious commandment, and whose calendar never touches our own. The real-world years here are a projection and are flagged as one everywhere they appear: no Herbert text gives an Earth date, so the anchor is the Dune Encyclopedia's Terran chronology, the only reference work that maps Terran events onto B.G. dates; anchored on 1588 CE = 14,512 B.G. and 1945 CE = 14,255 B.G. it puts A.G. 0 at roughly 16,100-16,200 CE, and I take 16,200, which sets the Jihad at 16,000, the novel's 10,191 A.G. at 26,391 and Chapterhouse at 41,440. Everything carries about a century of uncertainty from the Encyclopedia alone, and far more if non-canon material is rejected. Tier coverage follows the projection: no T2 events, because the fiction jumps from its founding straight to the novel ten thousand years later, and T4 consists of one Terran touchstone the Dune Encyclopedia preserves plus the 1965 publication, which is where this branch's real-world anchor actually lives.

lineages.title: Foundation
lineages.creator: Isaac Asimov

divergence.label: The founding of the Galactic Empire
divergence.delta: Real: the year 35,000 is empty - no human being has ever lived then and our record stops in the 21st century. Fiction: the same year is where the Galactic Era calendar begins, as the Trantorian Empire finishes absorbing the galaxy and is proclaimed the Galactic Empire - a state that stands twelve thousand years, then falls in a single lifetime, and whose fall Hari Seldon's psychohistory is built to shorten from thirty thousand years of barbarism to one thousand.
divergence.note: A projection, flagged as one, and resting on an inference as well. No Asimov text gives a real-world year for G.E. 1, and none states outright that G.E. 1 is the Empire's founding - that identification is reference-work inference from Frankenn I being called the first Emperor in Pebble in the Sky. The projection used is the only one Asimov himself published: his notebook chart in Thrilling Wonder Stories (Winter 1955) puts the hyperspatial drive at about 5,000 CE, 'Trantor becomes the Galactic Empire officially, about 35,000', Seldon's birth at about 47,000 and the Second Galactic Empire at 48,000. That scheme is corroborated twice by in-universe numerals - Seldon born 11,988 G.E. and the plan's thousand years counted from 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E. - so I use real = G.E. + 34,999, giving 12,069 G.E. = 47,068 and the Second Empire's due date at 48,067. It is flatly irreconcilable with the Robot/Foundation merger Asimov wrote in 1982-86, which implies G.E. 1 at about 11,600-12,100 CE and would move every date here back by some 23,400 years; the alternative is a different dataset row, not a rounding error, and is not blended in. Asimov's own comment on his dating was that it was 'made up ad hoc'.

ending.why: Asimov left the choice between a Second Empire and Galaxia open; the Plan is on schedule and its ending is deliberately unwritten.

events.title: 'Foundation' is published
events.description: The first story of the series appears in Astounding Science Fiction, written from August 1941 after Asimov's meeting with John W. Campbell; the fix-up novel follows in 1951 with 'The Psychohistorians' written last, to open a book whose first part was the last written.
events.note: The only real-world event in this lineage. It matters to the dating because the stories were written 1941-1949 as a far-future history with no real-world anchor at all; Asimov published a real-world scheme only in 1955.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Galactic Empire is founded
events.description: The Trantorian Empire becomes the Galactic Empire: Frankenn I is crowned, the Galactic Era calendar begins, and the Empire will hold the galaxy for twelve thousand years - the long peace whose end Seldon spends his life calculating.
events.note: Real year projected; the identification of G.E. 1 with the Empire's founding is reference-work inference, not an Asimov statement.
events.binWhy: Independent powers become one polity.

facets.change: expanding kingdom → galactic empire proclaimed

events.title: Pebble in the Sky
events.description: The Empire is still expanding at fifty new provinces a day, and Earth - the forgotten homeworld, its crust still radioactive from wars nobody remembers - is a backwater prison world where a man from the 20th century wakes up. It is the one Empire novel that prints a Galactic Era date.
events.note: The numeral is in the text ('in the Year of the Galactic Era 827'), which makes the in-universe date unusually solid; the real year is projected. The same novel is internally inconsistent, having a character estimate he was thrown 50,000 years forward.
events.binWhy: An empire still adding fifty provinces a day.

facets.change: empire → still adding provinces; the homeworld forgotten

events.title: Prelude to Foundation: Seldon comes to Trantor
events.description: Hari Seldon arrives on the imperial capital and presents psychohistory at the Decennial Convention - the moment the science that could save the galaxy becomes visible to the Empire that will want it suppressed.
events.note: 12,020 G.E. is Prelude's date. An early draft of the research brief attributed it to 'The Encyclopedists'; it belongs here, and the Encyclopedists belong at 50 F.E.
events.binWhy: Psychohistory is presented to the Empire and becomes visible.

facets.change: the fall unforeseen → a science that predicts it is presented

events.title: Seldon's trial and the exile to Terminus
events.description: Hari Seldon is tried by the Commission of Public Safety and exiled with his Encyclopedists to Terminus at the rim of the galaxy; the Foundation is founded there as a cover for the thousand-year plan to shorten the coming dark age from thirty thousand years to one.
events.note: The anchor is printed in the novel's own epigraph: Seldon 'born in the 11,988th year of the Galactic Era; died 12,069', the latter given as 'the year 1 F.E.'. The trial's year, 12,067, is the standard reading (Wikipedia and the chronologies agree). Real year projected.
events.binWhy: The Foundation is founded on Terminus under cover of exile.

facets.change: the scientist tried → exiled; the plan begins under cover

events.title: The Encyclopedists: the first Seldon Crisis
events.description: Fifty years after the founding, Terminus faces annexation by the neighbouring kingdom of Anacreon and survives it not by force but by playing its rivals off against each other - the pattern for every crisis to come, and the first proof that the plan works.
events.note: The story prints no G.E. numeral, only 'fifty years' since the Foundation was established; 50 F.E. follows from the epigraph's 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E. The brief's 'The Encyclopedists opens around 12,020 G.E.' is a mix-up: 12,020 is Prelude to Foundation, and 12,050 G.E. has no Encyclopedists connection in any source.
events.binWhy: Annexation is survived by diplomacy, not force.

facets.change: annexation threatened → survived by playing rivals off

events.title: The Mayors: religion instead of arms
events.description: Salvor Hardin breaks the Four Kingdoms by religion rather than by arms and the Foundation becomes the spiritual centre of its barbarian neighbours - 'violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.'
events.note: The F.E. year is fan-chronology rather than text; real year projected.
events.binWhy: Control of the neighbouring kingdoms is taken by religion rather than by arms.

facets.change: neighbours by arms → neighbours by religion

events.title: The Mule
events.description: A mutant outside psychohistory's equations conquers the Foundation and the remains of the Empire in five years, and the plan's first millennium looks lost - the one event Seldon's mathematics could not predict.
events.note: Fan-chronology year; real year projected.
events.binWhy: An enemy no one predicted conquers the Foundation in five years.

facets.change: the plan on course → an unpredicted mutant conquers everything

events.title: The Second Foundation is found
events.description: Search by the Foundation: the Second Foundation at Star's End is located and apparently destroyed, and the plan is restored - at the cost of the First Foundation believing itself alone in the galaxy.
events.note: Fan-chronology year; real year projected.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: hidden guardians → found, and apparently destroyed

events.title: Foundation's Edge: Trevize's choice
events.description: Five hundred years on, the two Foundations are on a collision course and Golan Trevize is made to choose the galaxy's future - Galaxia, a single group mind, over either of them.
events.note: Wikipedia dates the novel 'five hundred years after the establishment of the Foundation'; the F.E. numeral is fan-chronology.
events.binWhy: One man chooses a group mind for the galaxy.

facets.change: two foundations on collision → one man chooses a group mind

events.title: Foundation and Earth: the radioactive homeworld
events.description: Trevize's search ends on a radioactive Earth, the lost planet of origin, where he learns that the robot Daneel Olivaw has guided humanity for twenty thousand years and that the plan was never only Seldon's.
events.note: The 'twenty thousand years' is the novel's own wording - 'twenty thousand perhaps - since the people of the Galaxy have concerned themselves with Earth' - and it is the line that welds the Robot novels to the Foundation era, and therefore the line that makes Asimov's published 35,000 CE projection irreconcilable with the 1982-86 merger.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: origin lost → the homeworld found, and the hidden guide revealed

events.title: The Second Empire is due
events.description: The terminus of Seldon's plan: a Second Galactic Empire is to be founded a thousand years after the fall, thirty thousand years of barbarism compressed into one. The published stories stop five hundred years short of it.
events.note: Not a depicted event: this is psychohistory's own projection, the far end of the plan, included because it is the only date the fiction sets for its own future.
events.binWhy: The plan's terminus: a second empire a thousand years after the fall.

facets.change: thousand-year interregnum → a second empire due

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's 'history as engineering' case: an empire twelve thousand years old, a science that predicts its fall, and a plan to shorten thirty thousand years of barbarism to one thousand. It belongs here because its whole drama is the shape of a galactic civilisation's decline, and because its calendar is pure far-future: Galactic Era 1 is the founding of the Galactic Empire, and no Asimov text gives a real-world year for it, so every date here is a projection and is labelled as one. The projection used is the only one Asimov himself published - his 1955 notebook chart, which puts the Empire at about 35,000 CE, Seldon's birth at about 47,000 and the Second Empire at 48,000 - and it is corroborated twice by in-universe numerals (Seldon born 11,988 G.E.; 1 F.E. = 12,069 G.E.). It cannot be reconciled with the Robot/Foundation merger of 1982-86, which implies G.E. 1 at about 11,600-12,100 CE; that alternative belongs in a different row and is recorded in the divergence note rather than averaged in. Tier coverage reflects the projection: one T3 event (the 1942 first publication, the lineage's only real-world event), no T4 and no T2 events at all, and everything else in T1 between 35,000 and 48,000 CE. The fiction is silent about our own era by construction - its Earth survives only as a radioactive legend at the galaxy's edge, and no book dates it - which is why the lineage's contact with real history is a magazine issue rather than an event.

lineages.title: Warhammer 40,000
lineages.creator: Games Workshop

divergence.label: The Dark Age of Technology
divergence.delta: Real: the 15th millennium is empty - nothing human exists in it and our record stops in the 21st century. Fiction: M15 opens the Dark Age of Technology, in which humanity invents the warp drive, builds the Standard Template Construct, engineers the Navigator gene, records its first psykers and spreads a technological civilisation across the galaxy - the golden age whose collapse produces the Imperium of the 41st millennium, and which the Imperium itself no longer remembers.
divergence.note: The one branch in this group whose calendar is literally ours: Imperial dates are Anno Domini on the Gregorian calendar, and Games Workshop says so - the years 'are based on the Anno Domini system, so the dates themselves are the ones that we are familiar with now' - so nothing needs converting except millennium notation. Year N of millennium MN is (N-1)x1000+N AD: 798.M30 = 29,798 CE, 005.M31 = 30,005 CE, 999.M41 = 40,999 CE, 012.M42 = 41,012 CE, and real 2025 is 025.M3. The lore's Age of Terra (M1-M15) explicitly includes real human history, so the branch is identical to ours through the present. Where it first departs is genuinely arguable and no source names a date: some material has humanity settling the Sol System in the late 2nd/early 3rd millennium and launching sublight colony ships in the mid-to-late M3, which would put the fork a few centuries from now; the Dark Age of Technology's start is M15 in the 6th-edition rulebook but M21 in the 3rd-edition 'Journal of Keeper Cripias'; and the rupture the setting itself remembers is the Cybernetic Revolt and Old Night in M23-M25. I take M15, the first era boundary in the current timeline that is not our history. A reader who prefers the earlier reading should move the fork a few centuries ahead and treat M15 as deep. Two further disputes are carried in the events below: the millennium boundary itself (M41 runs 40,001-41,000 in most sources, 40,000-40,999 in the 5th-edition rulebook - 999.M41 = 40,999 either way), and the deliberately unresolvable question of what year the setting's present actually is.

ending.why: There is only war: a dying Imperium, a broken galaxy, and a setting built so that nothing can ever get better.

events.title: The Emperor is born
events.description: In a Neolithic village on the Sakarya river in Anatolia a being is born who will live for forty thousand years. The lore inserts him into real prehistory, guiding human civilisation in secret long before he reveals himself - the branch's hidden presence in our own past.
events.note: Dated to c. 8,000 BC by Realm of Chaos: The Lost and the Damned (1990), a first-edition supplement still cited by current reference works, which note it is more than 48,000 years before M41. Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (1987) instead says 'over ten thousand years ago', a contradiction the wikis flag; hence low confidence.
events.binWhy: A being is born who will rule for forty thousand years.

facets.change: a village → a being born who will rule for forty thousand years

events.title: Rogue Trader is published
events.description: Games Workshop publishes Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, the first edition of the game - the real-world origin of the branch, and the point from which every date above is written forward into a future that uses our own calendar.
events.note: A real-world publication event, not an in-universe one; it sits in the branch's prehistory because the fiction's own history is still ours in 1987.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Dark Age of Technology begins
events.description: Over the next ten thousand years humanity invents the warp drive and the Gellar field, builds the Standard Template Construct, engineers the Navigator gene, records its first psykers and spreads across the galaxy - a civilisation later remembered, when it is remembered at all, as a golden age and blamed for everything that followed.
events.note: Start date disputed across editions (M15 in the 6th-edition rulebook; M21 in the 3rd-edition 'Keeper Cripias' account), and the Age of Terra is variously said to end in M15 or M18. M15 is the current-canon reading.
events.binWhy: Ten thousand years of invention and expansion.

facets.change: one world → ten thousand years of invention and expansion

events.title: The Cybernetic Revolt
events.description: The Men of Iron turn on their human masters; the revolt burns the worlds of the Dark Age of Technology and leaves humanity with a terror of its own thinking machines that hardens into the Imperium's absolute ban on artificial intelligence.
events.note: Lexicanum dates the revolt to M23; other passages place it at the end of the Dark Age of Technology, c. M25. No finer date exists anywhere in the lore.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: machine servants → revolt and burn the worlds

events.title: Old Night: the Age of Strife
events.description: The warp storms that follow the revolt cut every human world off from every other, psykers go mad or are possessed, and interstellar civilisation collapses. Terra is isolated for five thousand years, and the age that ends it is built on superstition and fear rather than knowledge.
events.note: Lexicanum and the 6th-edition rulebook begin the Age of Strife in M25; the 3rd-edition 'Keeper Cripias' account says M26. It ends in M30.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: connected worlds → cut off by storms for five thousand years

events.title: The Fall of the Aeldari
events.description: The Aeldari empire's pleasure cults give birth to Slaanesh: the birth-shock destroys the Aeldari homeworlds, tears the Eye of Terror open and clears the warp storms that had isolated humanity - which is why the Imperium's rise is possible at all.
events.note: No source gives a year for the Fall, only a millennium: Fandom places it early in the 30th millennium, Lexicanum's timeline files it under M30, and one page has Slaanesh awaking in the 29th millennium. 29,100 is a placeholder inside the M30 window, not a date.
events.binWhy: A birth-shock destroys the homeworlds and tears the warp open.

facets.change: an empire of pleasure → gives birth to a god that destroys it

events.title: The Unification Wars end
events.description: Terra comes under a single ruler: the last techno-barbarian states and gene-cults of Old Night are destroyed, and the Emperor turns outward for the first time.
events.note: Dateline given by Lexicanum and by Games Workshop's own Horus Heresy timeline; the wars began in the late M29 or early M30.
events.binWhy: Terra comes under one ruler for the first time.

facets.change: warring states → one ruler over the homeworld

events.title: The Treaty of Mars and the founding of the Imperium
events.description: The Emperor and the Mechanicum sign the Treaty of Mars at Olympus Mons: the Imperium of Man is formally founded, and the alliance of throne and machine-cult that still holds it together is struck.
events.binWhy: Independent powers become one polity.

facets.change: throne and machine-cult → a treaty founds the empire

events.title: The Great Crusade begins
events.description: The Space Marine Legions leave the Sol System to reunite the scattered human worlds, recovering the lost primarchs one by one over two centuries and destroying everything that will not join.
events.binWhy: A campaign of conquest begins.

facets.change: one world → legions leave to reconquer the rest

events.title: The Horus Heresy begins
events.description: The Isstvan III atrocity opens the civil war: the Warmaster and half the Legions turn on the Emperor, and the nine years that follow burn the Imperium's best armies and end the Great Crusade.
events.note: Lexicanum dates the Heresy 005.M31-014.M31 and labels the dates approximate; Games Workshop's own timeline has the Isstvan III betrayal running 005-006.M31.
events.binWhy: Civil war begins with half the legions turning.

facets.change: crusade → half the legions turn on the throne

events.title: The Siege of Terra and the Golden Throne
events.description: The siege ends with Horus dead and the Emperor entombed on the Golden Throne; the Imperium becomes a deathless theocracy that will spend the next ten thousand years waiting for its god to wake.
events.binWhy: The siege ends with the traitor dead and the Emperor entombed.

facets.change: civil war → the traitor dead, the ruler entombed alive

events.title: The War of the Beast
events.description: An Ork empire led by the Beast nearly takes Terra a thousand years after the Heresy; the Imperium survives, and the political reckoning that follows - the Beheading of 546.M32 - reshapes its ruling institutions.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: stability → an alien empire nearly takes the capital

events.title: The Age of Apostasy: the Reign of Blood
events.description: Goge Vandire seizes both spiritual and temporal power and the Imperium tears itself apart in a century of religious civil war, from which the Adepta Sororitas and the modern Ecclesiarchy emerge.
events.note: Lexicanum dates the Age of Apostasy to M36 only; the ca. 200.M36 start of the Reign of Blood comes from the Fandom timeline. Finer precision does not exist.
events.binWhy: One man seizes both spiritual and temporal power.

facets.change: divided offices → one man seizes church and state

events.title: The Fall of Cadia and the Great Rift
events.description: The 13th Black Crusade breaks Cadia and the Great Rift opens across the galaxy, splitting the Imperium in two and ending the long stalemate of the 41st millennium.
events.binWhy: The fortress world falls and the empire is cut in two.

facets.change: long stalemate → the fortress falls and the realm is cut in two

events.title: The Indomitus Crusade and the Plague Wars
events.description: Roboute Guilliman's Indomitus Crusade and the Plague Wars that follow: the setting's present, in which the Imperium holds half a galaxy and the date itself is in dispute.
events.note: The Plague Wars are dated ca. 012.M42 in the Dark Imperium novel; the Indomitus Crusade's length was retconned in 2021 from about a century to about twelve years, and Games Workshop still bills the setting as 'the 41st Millennium', so 'M42' is a wiki convenience: the Chronostrife makes the present deliberately undecidable.
events.binWhy: Wars without end in the setting's present.

facets.change: a realm cut in two → wars without end

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's terminal case: forty thousand years of human history whose founding rupture is not merely forgotten but suppressed - the Imperium does not know what the Dark Age of Technology was - and whose calendar is nevertheless our own. Warhammer 40,000 is the one branch here that needs no projection: Imperial dates are Anno Domini on the Gregorian calendar (year N of millennium MN is (N-1)x1000+N AD, so 999.M41 = 40,999 CE and 2025 = 025.M3), and the lore's Age of Terra explicitly includes real human history, which is why this lineage has both a T4 event (the Emperor's birth in 8,000 BC, hidden inside our prehistory) and a T3 one (the game's own publication in 1987) before its fork. Where it forks is arguable and no source names a date: some material settles the Sol System in the late 2nd/early 3rd millennium and launches sublight colony ships in the mid-to-late M3, the Dark Age of Technology's start is M15 in the 6th-edition rulebook but M21 in the 3rd-edition 'Keeper Cripias' account, and the rupture the setting remembers is Old Night in M25. I take M15, the first era boundary in the current timeline that is not our history, and record the alternatives in the divergence note. Because the fiction's beats are spaced by millennia, T2 is empty - between the game's publication and the 15th millennium the branch has no near-future events to chart - and T1 carries thirteen of the fifteen events, which is exactly what a setting whose present is the 41st millennium should look like.

lineages.title: Mass Effect
lineages.creator: BioWare (Casey Hudson, director; Drew Karpyshyn, lead writer of the first two games)

divergence.label: Prothean ruins are found on Mars
divergence.delta: Real: 2148 is 122 years away, and the real exploration of Mars's south polar deposits has found layered ice and nothing built. Fiction: a cache left by a species extinct for 50,000 years lies under Promethei Planum, and it teaches humanity faster-than-light travel within months.
divergence.inUniverse: 2148 CE (Codex; the games use the Common Era calendar)
divergence.note: The games date everything in CE, so the fiction's years are ours. Up to 2147 its Earth follows a plausible projection of ours: a Moon settlement in 2069, the first permanent Mars settlement in 2103, helium-3 from Saturn in 2137. The first thing that cannot happen in our universe is the Mars find. The timeline notes traces of element zero on Mars in 2147, a year earlier; that is the first sign of the same discovery and is folded into it. The lore also has a long fictional galactic past that no human could see: the Protheans' fall around 48,000 BCE, the Citadel Council founded in 500 BCE, the geth uprising in 1895. None of it touches Earth's record before 2148, so it is left out of the chain rather than filed as prehistory.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mass Effect (video game) - set in 2183

ending.why: Whichever of Destroy, Control or Synthesis the player chooses, the Crucible stops the Reapers, and the Extended Cut shows the relays repaired and the species rebuilding; only the Refuse option added later lets the harvest run on, with the next cycle winning.

events.title: Mass Effect is released
events.description: BioWare's Mass Effect comes out on the Xbox 360, published by Microsoft Game Studios and planned from the start as the first part of a trilogy. It is the real-world origin of the branch.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mass Effect (video game) - set in 2183

events.note: Released 20 November 2007 (Xbox 360); Windows followed on 28 May 2008. Directed by Casey Hudson with Drew Karpyshyn as lead writer. A publication event, not an in-universe one; it sits in prehistory because the fiction's Earth is still ours in 2007.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Mass Effect 3 is released
events.description: The third game closes Commander Shepard's trilogy. Its ending, a choice between three uses of the Crucible, was badly received, and BioWare answered with a free Extended Cut that June.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mass Effect 3 - set in 2186; endings and Extended Cut

events.note: Released 6 March 2012; the Extended Cut, which expanded the ending slides and added the Refuse option, came out on 26 June 2012. A real-world publication event.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: A Prothean cache is found under the Martian south pole
events.description: Explorers find a small cache of technology left by the Protheans, a species extinct for some fifty thousand years, deep beneath Promethei Planum on Mars. Working from it, human scientists learn mass-effect physics within months and build the first faster-than-light drives.
events.note: Dated 2148 in the games' Codex and the fan wiki's timeline, which heads the year 'Humanity Discovers Mass Effect Physics'. The fiction's calendar is ours (CE), so nothing is converted. The year before, 2147, the timeline records trace amounts of element zero found on Mars, the first hint of the same discovery. The real Promethei Planum is a real region of Mars's south polar deposits; nothing has been found under it.
events.binWhy: The cache is a scientific windfall: the discovery hands humanity a physics it did not have, and everything later turns on it. It is also proof that non-human intelligence existed, but the Protheans are long dead; the living first contact comes in 2157 and is binned there.

facets.change: no FTL → mass-effect physics from an alien cache

events.title: Charon turns out to be a mass relay
events.description: Following the Mars data, a team near Pluto finds that its moon Charon is a dormant Prothean mass relay under kilometres of ice. Once it is switched on, Jon Grissom's crew goes through it to Arcturus, 36 light-years away, and finds a network that reaches across the galaxy. The same year, the eighteen largest nations on Earth sign the Systems Alliance charter.
events.note: Both the relay and the Alliance charter are dated 2149 in the timeline. They are merged here because the atlas allows one event per year, and the relay is the moment the Alliance was formed to exploit. Real Charon is a moon of Pluto, 1,212 km across, discovered in 1978.
events.binWhy: A passage to places unreachable is found and opened: one jump crosses 36 light-years.

facets.change: one star system → a galaxy-wide relay network

events.title: The first colonies beyond Sol are founded
events.description: The Delta Pavonis Foundation, an Earth consortium, starts settling Demeter, humanity's first colony outside the Solar System. Colonies on Eden Prime and Terra Nova follow the same year, with Alliance fleets and the station at Arcturus being built to defend them.
events.note: Dated 2152 in the timeline; the Alliance surveys that found Terra Nova are dated 2150 and construction at Arcturus 2151.
events.binWhy: Permanent settlements are founded on new worlds.

facets.change: Sol only → colonies on Demeter, Eden Prime and Terra Nova

events.title: Children exposed to element zero show telekinetic powers
events.description: Some of the children born after the 2151 element-zero accident at Singapore International Spaceport, where hundreds of people were exposed to the dust, begin to show minor telekinetic abilities. By 2158 the Alliance is tracking exposures and roughly one child in ten exposed shows biotic potential.
events.note: The timeline gives 2151 for the Singapore accident, 2156 for the first abilities and 2158 for humans learning 'the potential of biotics'. The atlas takes 2156, when the change appears. About 30% of the exposed children in Singapore developed cancers instead.
events.binWhy: Some humans are born with an ability no human had before, from exposure to an alien element.

facets.change: ordinary children → the first human biotics

events.title: The First Contact War with the turians
events.description: Turian ships catch human explorers switching on Relay 314, which Citadel law has forbidden since the Rachni Wars, and open fire. In a three-month war the turians take the colony of Shanxi and the Alliance Second Fleet takes it back; the Citadel Council then steps in, brokers peace and tells humanity that a galactic community exists.
events.inUniverse: 2157 CE; the Relay 314 Incident to the turians

sources.title: Mass Effect Wiki: First Contact War

events.note: Dated 2157 in the timeline; the war lasted about three months and killed 623 humans and slightly more turians. The turians call it the Relay 314 Incident and were ordered to pay reparations. An anonymous manifesto after the war calls for a 'Cerberus' to defend humanity, the origin of the Illusive Man's organisation.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets a living non-human intelligence for the first time. It is also a short war, but the war lasts three months and matters because it is the meeting; the major war in this branch comes in 2186.

facets.change: alone in the galaxy → one species among many, met by gunfire

events.title: Humanity is given an embassy on the Citadel
events.description: The Citadel Council formally recognises humanity's growing power and gives it an embassy on the Citadel, the station at the political and economic centre of the galaxy. Humans are now inside the Council's order, without a seat on the Council, and they are competing with the batarians for the Skyllian Verge.
events.note: Dated 2165 in the timeline. A 2164 assassination attempt on the volus ambassador had put the bid at risk. Humanity gets a Council seat only in 2183, after the Battle of the Citadel.
events.binWhy: Humanity joins the species that live under the Council's laws. It is an accession, not a founding, but it is the moment a single power enters a larger charter.

events.title: The Reapers invade, and the Crucible is fired
events.description: The Reapers invade through batarian space and attack Earth. There the Catalyst, the intelligence that made the Reapers, offers Shepard three uses of it: destroy all synthetic life with the Reapers, control the Reapers, or merge organic and synthetic life.

events.note: The third game is set in 2186 (Wikipedia). Everything to the end of the game happens in 2186, so the invasion and the Crucible are one event. The ending is the player's choice: Destroy kills the geth and EDI, Control makes Shepard the mind of the Reapers, Synthesis rewrites every living thing, and the Extended Cut added Refuse, in which the harvest goes on. T4, T3 and T1 are empty: the fiction's Earth matches ours until 2148, and the trilogy never goes past 2186.

lineages.creator: Ronald D. Moore (developer), from Glen A. Larson's 1978 series

divergence.label: The Thirteenth Tribe leaves Kobol
divergence.delta: Real: around 152,000 BCE anatomically modern humans live in small foraging groups in Africa, with no farming, writing or metal. Fiction: on Kobol, a world elsewhere in the galaxy, a starfaring human civilisation already exists, and its thirteenth tribe, which is in fact a people of humanoid machines, leaves to found a world it calls Earth. It is not our Earth; ours enters the story only at the end.
divergence.inUniverse: ca. 4,000 years before the Fall of the Twelve Colonies (radiocarbon dating of the Temple of Five, 'The Eye of Jupiter')
divergence.note: Conversion, stated explicitly. The series finale ('Daybreak', aired 20 March 2009) cuts from the fleet's arrival on our Earth to modern New York with the title '150,000 years later'; the modern scene is taken as 2009, the year it aired, so the arrival is 2009 - 150,000 = 147,991 BCE (year -147991). The fleet reaches the first, dead Earth about three years after the Fall ('Three years ago I promised to lead you to a new home', 'Revelations') and our Earth some weeks or months later, so the Fall is placed three years earlier, at year -147994, and dates given as 'N years before the Fall' (Battlestar Wiki's BCH) convert as -147994 - N. The single-year precision is an artefact of that arithmetic: '150,000 years' is a round figure. The date of the exodus itself is contradictory on screen: Tyrol's radiocarbon estimate gives at least 4,000 years, Elosha says all thirteen tribes left about 2,000 years ago ('Kobol's Last Gleaming'), and Cottle ties a virus to the Thirteenth Tribe's departure 'over 3,000 years ago' ('A Measure of Salvation'). The earliest figure is used because the fork has to precede everything fictional; Kobol's own history is older still and undated.

events.description: The fleet finds the Earth of legend a radioactive ruin, survives a mutiny, then jumps to coordinates Kara Thrace derives from a song and finds a green planet already home to primitive humans and names it Earth. Colonists and allied Cylons agree to start again with nothing, fly their ships into the Sun, and scatter across the continents; Hera, the first child of a human and a Cylon, becomes the ancestor of everyone alive today.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the space-opera archetype for its fleets, colonies and a war across star systems, but like Star Wars it runs in reverse: the finale's '150,000 years later' cut to modern New York places the whole story in our deep past, so epoch is deep-past. It follows the 2003 miniseries and the 2004-2009 series (with the season-4 revelations and the wiki's reconstructed day counts); the prequel Caprica is used only for context in notes. Tier coverage is lopsided by construction: every story event is T4 (about 152,000 to 148,000 BCE), the three T2 entries are the two releases and the 2009 epilogue, and T3 and T1 are empty because nothing happens between the landing and the present, and nothing after it. Phases are derived from the divergence; everything after the Thirteenth Tribe's exodus is 'deep' because the fork precedes the main story by about 4,000 years. Two machine uprisings are binned machine-awakens (the first Earth's and the Colonies'); the Fall itself is mass-death, because by then the Cylons are an established enemy, not a newly woken one.

lineages.title: Halo
lineages.creator: Bungie (2001-2010), then 343 Industries / Halo Studios; Forerunner prehistory by Greg Bear (novels, 2011-2013)

divergence.label: An ancient human civilisation is already spreading between the stars
divergence.delta: Real: around 150,000 BCE anatomically modern humans live in Africa as hunter-gatherers with stone tools, and nobody has left the planet. Fiction: an earlier humanity has an interstellar civilisation spreading along the Orion Arm, on its way to a war with the Forerunners that will end with its survivors stripped of their technology and exiled to Earth.
divergence.inUniverse: c. 150,000 BCE (Halopedia's earliest dated statement about the ancient human civilisation; its rise is not dated)
divergence.note: The UNSC story starts in the 2160s, but Halo's history leaves ours much earlier. In the canon as it now stands, today's humans descend from an interstellar people who fought the Flood and the Forerunners, were defeated around 106,445 BCE, devolved and confined to Earth, and were returned to Earth again after the Halo Array fired around 97,445 BCE. None of that is in our archaeological record, so under the rule that anything fictional comes after the fork, the fork has to sit in deep prehistory. No source dates the ancient civilisation's beginning; c. 150,000 BCE is the earliest year Halopedia attaches to it, and all these deep dates are approximate. Between 97,445 BCE and 2160 the Halo record is to all intents ours (its twenty-first-century entries are trivia, such as an engineering society founded in 2021 and a book in the 2004 alternate-reality game), so a reader interested only in the UNSC chronology can treat March 2160 as a practical second threshold.

sources.title: Halopedia: Human-Forerunner wars (c. 107,445-106,445 BCE; human civilisation on the Orion Arm c. 150,000 BCE)
Halopedia: Halo universe (overview of the canonical timeline)

ending.why: Humanity has won the Covenant War and outlived Cortana's rule, but as of Halo Infinite (2560) the UNSC Infinity is wrecked, the Banished hold Zeta Halo, and the war with them is unfinished.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in far-future space opera: a human interstellar state of hundreds of colonies at war with a multi-species alien theocracy, among the ruins of an older galactic civilisation. The continuity is the games' canon as maintained by 343 Industries / Halo Studios and catalogued by Halopedia, which folds in the novels (Greg Bear's Forerunner Saga supplies the ancient past). The Paramount+ television series (2022-2024) is a separate continuity and is not used. Tiers: three T4 events in deep prehistory (c. 150,000 to c. 97,445 BCE), all approximate; T3 is empty, because the fiction adds nothing to the twentieth century; T2 holds the two releases and the twenty-second and twenty-third centuries (the Interplanetary War, the Unified Earth Government and the slipspace drive); T1 holds everything from the colonisation of Reach in 2362 to Zeta Halo in 2559.

events.title: War comes to the colonies: the Jovian Moons Campaign
events.description: Humanity has settled Mars, the Jovian moons and the asteroids, and the colonies are fought over by the corporate-backed Friedens and the neo-communist Koslovics. The three-month campaign on the Jovian moons opens a decade of fighting, through the Rainforest Wars in South America to the Interplanetary War, in which the United Nations' new UNSC fights both.

events.description: Rebels in the Outer Colonies seize the UNSC corvette Callisto and destroy a pursuing destroyer with a nuclear device hidden in an asteroid. It is the usual start date for the Insurrection, an undeclared civil war between Earth and its colonies that lasts three decades.

events.title: The Covenant finds Harvest
events.description: An alien warship enters the Epsilon Indi system, and a first meeting on the colony of Harvest turns into a massacre. events.note: Halopedia: detected on 3 February 2525; the landing and first killing on 11 February; the destruction of the Harvest battle group on 7 October 2525, the war's formal start. By April 2526 the UNSC had turned from the Insurrection to the Covenant.

events.title: Reach falls, a Halo is destroyed, and the war is won at the Ark
events.description: The Covenant burn Reach and then find Earth. The wiki's own window is 2103-2758 for the epoch and 2800-3500 CE for the story; a reviewer reads it as roughly AD 3000, which this conversion matches (Red Rising opens in 3021). Anything before the colonisation, including a Third World War the saga mentions but never dates, is invisible.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in far-future space opera because its history is carried by starships, colonies on other worlds and a non-human maker species, across three centuries. events.inUniverse: 1327 CE (Consider Phlebas, 'A Short History of the Idiran War')

events.binWhy: Two interstellar civilisations go to war.

facets.change: uneasy neighbours → the largest war in fifty thousand years

events.title: The Twin Novae
events.description: In one of the last space battles of the war, two stars are made to explode, killing billions. The war in space ends the same year, and eight centuries later the light of the novae is still arriving at the orbital where Look to Windward is set.

events.binWhy: An act of war kills billions.

events.title: The Idiran War ends
events.description: The war ends formally forty-eight years and one month after it began, with the Culture the winner. The appendix counts 851.4 billion dead, 91 million starships, fourteen thousand orbitals and six stars destroyed.

events.binWhy: One side wins the war outright.

facets.change: a war in the balance → a Culture victory

events.title: The Excession, and a war arranged on purpose
events.description: The black sphere reappears at the edge of Culture space and resists every attempt to probe it. A group of Culture Minds lets the cruel, expanding Affront steal mothballed Culture warships, to give the Culture an excuse for war. A hidden fleet meets them, the sphere lashes out and then vanishes, and the brief war stops.

events.binWhy: A war between civilisations, provoked in secret by one side's own Minds.

facets.change: a watched stand-off → a war provoked on purpose

events.title: A Culture ship studies Earth and leaves it alone
events.description: The Contact ship Arbitrary spends months studying Earth: its broadcasts, its weapons and its politics. One of the crew argues for contact to repair the mess humanity has made; another wants to wipe the species out. The Culture leaves the planet alone, and no one on Earth learns that it was there.

events.title: The Empire of Azad falls after its game
events.description: Gurgeh, a bored Culture game-player blackmailed into service, travels to an empire where a single game decides rank and the throne. In the final against the Emperor, on a planet swept by periodic fire, the Emperor dies by a shot from his own gun, and the empire collapses without further help. Gurgeh learns he was a pawn in the Culture's plan.

events.title: The Culture contacts Earth

events.title: A Chelgrian assassin comes to Masaq' Orbital
events.description: The Culture's meddling set off a caste war on Chel. In revenge, a grieving officer, Quilan, is sent to Masaq' Orbital with his memory edited, carrying wormholes for a strike on its Hub Mind. The Hub already knows, and suspects that the 'aliens' behind the plot were warlike Culture Minds. At the concert marking the Twin Novae, Mind and assassin end their lives together.

events.binWhy: A suicide attack aimed at one specific target, a habitat's governing Mind.

facets.change: a planned revenge → a Mind and its assassin dying together

events.title: The Gzilt Sublime
events.description: The Gzilt, a civilisation that nearly helped found the Culture, leave the material universe together for the Sublime. In their last weeks, a secret about the origins of their holy book threatens to come out, and a Gzilt warship destroys the envoy sent to confess it.
events.inUniverse: about 1,000 years after the Idiran War (The Hydrogen Sonata)

events.title: The War in Heaven comes out of the simulation
events.description: For decades, a war game run in simulation has been deciding whether civilisations may keep virtual Hells for the minds of their dead. When the pro-Hell side cheats and takes the war into the real world, Culture agents make sure the attack destroys the Hells, while appearing to try to stop it.
events.inUniverse: 'six hundred years' after Look to Windward (Surface Detail)

events.note: The latest dated Culture story, and the least certain date. Surface Detail says Look to Windward happened 'six hundred years ago' (c. 2767), but also puts the Idiran War about 1,500 years back (c. 2875). Banks said in a 2010 interview that it is set about 800 years after Look to Windward (c. 2967-70). I use the first, most specific textual anchor.
events.binWhy: The conflict over the Hells is settled: the Hells are destroyed and the anti-Hell side wins.

facets.change: a war over the dead fought in simulation → the Hells destroyed in reality

lineages.groupingNote: The archetype's post-scarcity utopia: an interstellar civilisation of humans and artificial Minds that intervenes, covertly and at a scale of centuries, in the societies it meets. It belongs here because its drama is galactic politics and war over thousands of years. It follows Banks's published chronology, taking the novels' own cross-references (the Consider Phlebas appendix's 1327-1375 CE for the Idiran War, then the later books' 'N years after the war') as the Wikipedia Culture-series table and the Wertzone chronology lay them out. The anchors are Consider Phlebas (1327, 1331, 1375), The Player of Games (c. 2083-88), The State of the Art and Use of Weapons (1977 and 2092), Excession (c. 1867 and c. 633 BCE), Look to Windward (c. 2167), The Hydrogen Sonata (c. 2375) and Surface Detail (c. 2767). Matter (c. 1887 or 2167, self-contradictory) and Inversions (undated) are left out. Tier coverage: T4 for the founding, the first sighting of the Excession, the Idiran War and Excession; T3 for Earth in 1977 and the 1987 publication; T2 for Azad, Earth contact and Masaq' (2087-2167); T1 for the Gzilt Subliming and Surface Detail (2375-2767).
